summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app for myself, and the interesting work lately has been less "add a feature" and more "prove the feature is actually teaching what I think it's teaching." I added a question form (〜ますか) to the grammar engine — turns out the app had 211 verb frames and not one of them was phrased as a question, so the whole "chat with a persona" feature couldn't ask anything back. Fixing that meant adding a fourth axis to how the engine composes sentence forms, plus handling something English does structurally differently: a question fronts its auxiliary past the subject, and nothing in the existing sentence-assembly code expected that.

A lot of the rest has been chasing down guards that look like they're checking something but aren't. One test asserted a rate — "how often does the engine's distractor pool overlap" — and it was calibrated back when the catalogue was 15 sentence frames. By the time it grew to 51, the test still passed, but it had quietly stopped measuring the thing it was named for. I've hit that same failure shape enough times now (a docstring claiming "every check goes through here" when it doesn't, a dedupe keyed on the wrong field, a fallback path that silently reproduces the exact behavior a change was supposed to remove) that I keep a running log of them, because the pattern itself is more useful than any single fix.

On the audio side, I run VOICEVOX (Japanese text-to-speech) locally and treat every synthesized clip as something to verify, not trust — a mechanical check compares the expected pronunciation against what the engine actually produced before anything ships. That caught real bugs (words getting mis-read because of ambiguity in the kana), but chasing one refusal down taught me the opposite lesson too: most of the time the engine's right and my expectation is wrong, so the discipline is "figure out which side is actually wrong," not "override the checker."

I also did a short, unrelated build for a job transition — a self-contained farewell page in English and Japanese, audio included, that works offline on any device. Small, but a good reminder that a two-language deliverable has its own failure modes: a CSS grid layout was silently splitting a sentence character-by-character down a 13px column, and it looked enough like intentional vertical Japanese typesetting that nobody caught it by eye.
